## Hiring and jobs

**Hiring as a negotiation.** Today a king asks for candidates, up to three random free characters pitch from wherever they are, kings bid blind, and the highest bid at or above the asking price wins. Nobody travels, nobody haggles, and nobody learns there was a bidding war. Instead:

- **Characters travel to volunteer,** to courts that are hiring, where their sympathy lies, or away from danger, and the journey takes time like an envoy's.
- **They pitch in person and can play courts against each other:** "the king of Babylon offered me 30 shekels." It may be true or a lie.
- **Checking takes time, and the candidate may not wait.** A background check or a question to one's own envoy at Babylon takes seasons, and meanwhile the character may move on to another court. The king weighs verifying against losing the candidate. One round of negotiation a season; holding out costs the character time too.
- **Punishment has a price.** A king who catches a liar may execute him and take his purse and whatever he carried. But the execution spreads as a rumour, carried by whoever was at court, and characters grow wary of that court: the timid stay away, and the rest ask more to come. Harshness deters cheats and frightens honest talent alike; leniency attracts both. Executing someone whose claim turns out to be true is worse still. Gentler options exist: dismissing him, or exposing the lie to other courts, which damages his reputation instead of the king's.

**Fees clear the market (decided 21 October 2026).** No rule sets the price of work. Characters are hired for jobs with a fee ("Jobs, not wages"), and every fee is what the two sides agree ("Hiring as a negotiation"), with no rate or floor set by the engine (decided 28 October 2026): what others were paid is only what a character has heard, and he bargains from it. When demand is greater than supply, employers outbid each other and the fees agreed rise; when supply is greater, they fall. The able are always scarce ("Enough people, not enough good ones"), so their price rises furthest.

**Anyone can hire anyone (decided 21 October 2026).** Hiring is one contract whoever pays: a king, a city-state or a character, with the same jobs and fees, offers, loyalty and quitting ("Jobs, not wages"). A character pays his people from his purse or hoard, wherever his gold is; one who does not pay what he promised gets the name of it, and his people leave him as they would leave a king. This is what lets enterprise grow: a dealer hires a guard for the road, a lender an agent to collect from a debtor, a captain the men of his band, a rich man a spy on the king who owes him. Hiring is for named people, the characters. Soldiers are not characters but men in a unit: a power levies them from its land, and a character gathers them into a band ("Bands are a character's soldiers"). What stays with powers is what comes from holding land: levies, garrisons and sealing for a kingdom.

**Working for oneself (decided 21 October 2026).** A character's outside option is to serve no king. Characters already play for wealth ("Stakes, not dispositions"), so each compares what service pays with what he can earn on his own: dealing with other characters ("Characters deal with each other"), selling news ("Characters as sellers of news"), lending ("Lending to kings", "Lending to anyone"), forging on commission, mercenary work and escorting, interpreting at a posted price ("A go-between for hire"), ransom brokering, and outlawry ("Turning outlaw", "Pirates and bandits"). When fees are low, enterprise pays better and characters leave service; when kings pay well, they come back. Nobody is told to become a merchant: it pays or it does not. Two conditions. Enterprise must pay enough to be chosen but not so much that no king can hire, which the first guesses must leave room for and item 18 tunes. And script characters choose between service and enterprise by comparing expected income, or the feature does not count as built ("Every feature is every seat's"). A character working for himself can employ others too ("Anyone can hire anyone").

**Work on any terms.** Characters are hired for jobs as "Jobs, not wages" sets out, or, for a merchant, for a share of the gain. Only the fee, its split and any conditions, such as a deadline, a place or amounts, are structured, so the engine can check them; everything else stays words. A job may be agreed by word or by tablet: a sealed job tablet lets a cheated man prove his case to others, where a job agreed by word is his word against his employer's ("By word or by tablet"). A recipient named to pay the rest never promised anything himself, so his refusal breaks no promise and costs him little; that risk is the carrier's. The split prices trust both ways: a man with a good name can ask for the fee up front, a king known to pay can pay later, and strangers meet halfway. Nothing carries interest unless the words say so. A fee left unpaid is a default like any other: it touches no score ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice"), and the world answers it: the character gives notice or turns, sells what he knows, and word spreads, so that employer must offer more next time.

**If-clauses in contracts (decided 21 October 2026).** A job, a loan or any agreement may carry a few flat conditional clauses, in the same engine-checkable vocabulary as scheduled orders ("Scheduled, conditional orders" under Pacing): tablet sealed, envoy returned, city held, amount delivered, season reached. "If a tablet is sealed with Babylon by the next harvest, the rest is twenty minas; otherwise five." Two or three clauses at most and no nesting, so contracts stay readable to players, easy for script characters to evaluate, and safe from being turned into puzzles that exploit the engine. It is the native grammar of the age: Hammurabi's laws are a long list of "if a man does this, then that", and contracts and loans carried such clauses. A contract never pays itself: paying stays a separate act, and the engine registers whether the promise was kept. An employer may back his word with a scheduled payment that fires when the condition is met, so a sleeping king keeps his promise without waking; whether he does is his choice, and a court known to pay on time is worth more to serve. Clauses can bind the worker too ("if the delivery is short, the advance is returned"), which is his promise, kept or not like any other.

**What the advance is for.** Nothing says how a fee should be split, but there is a natural point: the advance covers what the job costs on the road, food, escort, tolls and a living abroad, so the worker risks only his time, and the rest is his profit. An advance below the costs means the worker finances the job from his own purse, and he asks more for it; one above them is a sign of trust. Script characters compare the advance with the costs they expect, and model characters weigh it for themselves. The period knew the pattern: messengers set out with provisions, the host court fed them abroad, and Old Assyrian merchants travelled on capital their partners advanced.
